questions.knowledge_point: Determining the Sign of a Circulation From a Diagram
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14060266/assets/6ed50407066da9fc213202ccff8c8be06c89d2dce0f5dfe07877cab77c98b3ec.png)

Consider the ellipse $E$ and vector field $F$ shown above. Let $C$ be any path where $E$ is traversed once in the **clockwise** direction. Which of the following statements are true?

- ${∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r<0$
- ${∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r>0$
- ${∮}_{-C}F\cdot \text{d}r=0$
questions.worked_solution:
The circulation $Γ$ measures the total work done by a force $F$ in moving a particle along a *closed* curve $C.$
It is given by the formula

$$
Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

We now recall the following:

- If the force works *with* the motion of the particle (i.e., the force helps to push the particle along the path), then ${∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r>0.$

- If the force works *against* the motion of the particle (i.e., the force impedes the motion of the particle as it moves along the path), then ${∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r<0.$

With that in mind, let's check each statement.

- Statements I and II are false. Since the force $F$ acts perpendicular to the motion of the particle as it moves around $C,$ it neither helps nor hinders its motion. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14060266/assets/045f6867a50dff0c162376015cc4651de796d0a637643b4b5ba402ef55dde4fa.png)

So, ${∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r=0.$

- Statement III is true. If we reverse the orientation of $C,$ then the situation with regards to the work done by $F$ remains unchanged.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14060266/assets/698f68b9539e6ef5c4b07dbe6cf3859449e2687db19406f6c2b0072fa5eb697e.png)

So, ${∮}_{-C}F\cdot \text{d}r=0.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only."

questions.problem: Calculate the circulation $Γ$ of the vector field $F(x,y)=\frac{3}{y}\,i-\frac{2}{x}\,j$ along the ellipse $C$ with equation $9{x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}=36$ oriented counterclockwise.
questions.worked_solution:
First, we write the equation of our curve as

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{3}^{2}}=1.
$$

The closed curve $C$ is the ellipse centered at the origin with horizontal and vertical semiaxes $2$ and $3,$ respectively. It can be parameterized in the counterclockwise direction as

$$
r(t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

The circulation $Γ$ measures the total work done by a force $F$ in moving a particle along a *closed* curve $C.$
It is given by the formula

$$
Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=3\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =\frac{3}{y}\,i-\frac{2}{x}\,j \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\,i-\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,j \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\,i-\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\,j)\cdot (-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j) \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\cdot (-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)-\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\cdot 3\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =-2-3 \\  & =-5.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(-5)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-5t\,{|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =-5(2\pi )-0 \\  & =-10\pi \end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Calculate the circulation $Γ$ of the vector field $F(x,y)=x\,i+y\,j$ along the closed curve $C$ given by $r(t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j$ for $t\in [0,2\pi ).$
questions.worked_solution:
The circulation $Γ$ measures the total work done by a force $F$ in moving a particle along a *closed* curve $C.$
It is given by the formula

$$
Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=3\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =x\,i+y\,j \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,j \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j)\cdot (-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j) \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot (-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot 3\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =5\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }5\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{5}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{5}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{5}{2}(\frac{-\operatorname{cos}⁡2t}{2})\,{|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =\frac{5}{4}(-1+1) \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Calculate the circulation $Γ$ of the vector field $F(x,y)=\frac{1}{y}\,i-\frac{1}{x}\,j$ along the closed curve $C$ given by $r(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j$ for $t\in [0,2\pi ).$
questions.worked_solution:
The circulation $Γ$ measures the total work done by a force $F$ in moving a particle along a *closed* curve $C.$
It is given by the formula

$$
Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =\frac{1}{y}\,i-\frac{1}{x}\,j \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\,i-\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,j \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\,i-\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\,j)\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j) \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+(-\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡t})\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =-1-1 \\  & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(-2)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-2t\,{|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =-2(2\pi )-0 \\  & =-4\pi \end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Calculate the circulation $Γ$ of the vector field $F(x,y)=y\,i-x\,j$ along the closed curve $C$ given by $r(t)=\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j$ for $t\in [0,2\pi ).$
questions.worked_solution:
The circulation $Γ$ measures the total work done by a force $F$ in moving a particle along a *closed* curve $C.$
It is given by the formula

$$
Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =y\,i-x\,j \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i-\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,j \\  & =-\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i-\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j)\cdot (-\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j) \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot (-\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)-\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =-\sqrt{3}{sin}^{2}⁡t-\sqrt{3}{cos}^{2}⁡t \\  & =-\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(-\sqrt{3})\,\text{d}t \\  & =-\sqrt{3}t\,{|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =-\sqrt{3}(2\pi )-0 \\  & =-2\pi \sqrt{3}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Calculate the circulation $Γ$ of the vector field $F(x,y)=\frac{5}{y}\,i+\frac{1}{x}\,j$ along the ellipse $C$ with equation $25{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=25$ oriented counterclockwise.
questions.worked_solution:
First, we write the equation of our curve as

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{1}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{5}^{2}}=1.
$$

The closed curve $C$ is the ellipse centered at the origin with horizontal and vertical semiaxes $1$ and $5,$ respectively. It can be parameterized in the counterclockwise direction as

$$
r(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+5\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

The circulation $Γ$ measures the total work done by a force $F$ in moving a particle along a *closed* curve $C.$
It is given by the formula

$$
Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=5\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =\frac{5}{y}\,i+\frac{1}{x}\,j \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\,i+\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,j \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+5\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\,i+\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\,j)\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+5\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j) \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\cdot 5\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =-1+5 \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }4\,\text{d}t \\  & =4t\,{|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =4(2\pi )-0 \\  & =8\pi \end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the scalar field $f(x,y)={y}^{2}\operatorname{arctan}⁡x.$ Which of the following statements are true?

- $∇f$ is conservative
- ${\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r=0$ for any piecewise smooth path $C\in {R}^{2}$
- ${∮}_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r=0$ for any closed path $C\in {R}^{2}$
questions.worked_solution:
If $F$ is a conservative vector field on ${R}^{2},$ then the circulation $Γ=0$ for any *closed* path $C\in {R}^{2},$ that is 

$$
Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r=0.
$$

With that in mind, let's consider each statement in turn:

- Statement I is true. The vector field $∇f$ is conservative by definition.

- Statement II is false, while statement III is true. The result $Γ=0$ applies to closed curves only.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Determining the Sign of a Circulation From a Diagram
canonical_examples.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14060266/assets/f7e61f72ed7488fd490f42ff519316ed2e87d3c997d64e2cc6b7af36f951dbb5.png)

Consider the circle $S$ and vector field $\mathbf F,$ shown above. Let $C$ be any path where $S$ is traversed once in the counterclockwise direction. Which of the following statements are true?

- $\displaystyle\oint_C\mathbf F\cdot \textrm d \mathbf r =  0$

- $\displaystyle\oint_C\mathbf F\cdot \textrm d \mathbf r > 0$

- $\displaystyle\oint_{-C}\mathbf F\cdot \textrm d \mathbf r > 0$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The circulation $\Gamma$ measures the total work done by a force $\mathbf F$ in moving a particle along a *closed* curve $C.$
It is given by the formula

$$
\Gamma = \oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \textrm{d} \mathbf r
= \int_a^b \mathbf F(r(t)) \cdot \mathbf r'(t) \; \textrm{d}t.
$$

We now recall the following:

- If the force works *with* the motion of the particle (i.e., the force helps to push the particle along the path), then $\displaystyle\oint_C\mathbf F\cdot \textrm d \mathbf r > 0.$

- If the force works *against* the motion of the particle (i.e., the force impedes the motion of the particle as it moves along the path), then $\displaystyle\oint_C\mathbf F\cdot \textrm d \mathbf r <                               0.$

With that in mind, let's check each statement.

- Statement I is true, while statement II is false. Since the force $\mathbf F$ acts perpendicular to the motion of the particle as it moves around $C,$ it neither helps nor hinders its motion. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14060266/assets/063836a4780ecb4be6e8c6149a422e3c8e9f2770304e659a8116691b91e3d7f1.png)

So, $\displaystyle\oint_C\mathbf F\cdot \textrm d \mathbf r = 0.$

- Statement III is false. If we reverse the orientation of $C,$ then the situation with regards to the work done by $\mathbf F$ remains unchanged.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14060266/assets/704915d2852e1654aa31d17bd2dfb07a3022fe3d8b597f37bf98bd5af2de1d1b.png)

So, $\displaystyle\oint_{-C}\mathbf F\cdot \textrm d \mathbf r = 0.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

canonical_examples.problem: Calculate the circulation $\Gamma$ of the vector field $\mathbf F(x,y) = -y\,\mathbf{i} +x\,\mathbf{j}$ along the circle $C$ with equation $x^2 + y^2 = 1,$ oriented counterclockwise.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The closed curve $C$ is the unit circle. It can be parameterized in the counterclockwise direction as

$$
\mathbf{r}(t) = \cos{t}\,\mathbf{i} + \sin{t}\,\mathbf{j},
\qquad 0 \leq t \lt 2\pi.
$$

The circulation $\Gamma$ measures the total work done by a force $\mathbf F$ in moving a particle along a *closed* curve $C.$
It is given by the formula

$$
\Gamma = \oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \textrm{d} \mathbf r
= \int_a^b \mathbf F(r(t)) \cdot \mathbf r'(t) \; \textrm{d}t.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x = \cos t, \qquad
y = \sin t.
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))=-y\,i+x\,j=-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $\mathbf r'(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,j \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j)\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j) \\  & ={sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
Consider the vector field $\mathbf F(x,y) =( e^y+x)\,\mathbf i +(xe^y+y^2)\,\mathbf j.$ Which of the following statements are true?

- $\mathbf F$ is conservative

- $\displaystyle\int\limits_C\mathbf F \cdot \textrm d\mathbf r = 0$ for any piecewise-smooth path $C\in\mathbb R^2$

- $\displaystyle\oint\limits_C\mathbf F \cdot \textrm d\mathbf r =0$ for any closed path $C\in\mathbb R^2$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
If $\mathbf F$ is a conservative vector field on $\mathbb R^2,$ then the circulation $\Gamma = 0$ for any *closed* path $C\in\mathbb R^2,$ that is 

$$
\Gamma = \oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \textrm{d} \mathbf r = 0.
$$

We notice that $\mathbf F = P\,\mathbf i + Q\,\mathbf j$ is a vector field with domain $D = \mathbb R^2.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we have

$$
\dfrac{\partial P}{\partial y} = \dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial x} =  e^y.
$$

With that in mind, let's consider each statement.

- Statement I is true. The vector field $\mathbf F$ is conservative since the partial derivatives are equal and continuous everywhere on $\mathbb R^2.$

- Statement II is false, while statement III is true. The result $\Gamma = 0$ applies to closed curves only.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."
